turns.content: Doctor: Hello—I'm Dr. Agent. Can you tell me your age and when the rash started (how many days/weeks ago)? Patient:
Patient: I’m 47 years old, and the rash started just last night—so it’s been about one day.

Doctor: Thank you—can you describe what the rash looks like (color, spots vs blisters, flat vs raised) and where it started/what areas are involved? Also, do you have fever, sore throat, or any new medication/illness or recent insect sting/cosmetic/plant exposure in the last week?

Patient: The rash is on the upper half of my back and looks like red patches, fairly flat, without blisters or obvious open sores. I don’t have fever, sore throat, or trouble breathing, and I haven’t started any new medications or had any new plant, cosmetic, or insect sting exposure in the past week. I also have mucositis along with my new cough, which is making me especially worried.

Doctor: I’m hearing a rapidly started, flat red patch rash on the upper back (1 day), plus mucositis and a new cough without fever or breathing trouble—can you confirm whether the mucositis includes mouth sores/ulcers or lip swelling, and whether you have any eye redness, genital sores, or skin tenderness? Also, have you noticed any rapidly spreading rash beyond the back or any dark/purple bruiselike spots?

Patient: Yes—my mucositis feels like painful mouth sores/ulcers in my mouth, but I haven’t noticed lip swelling. I don’t have eye redness, genital sores, or skin tenderness, and the rash hasn’t spread rapidly beyond my upper back; I also haven’t seen any dark or purple bruiselike spots.

Doctor: Given the timing (1 day), location (upper back), flat red patches, and painful mouth ulcers with a new cough (without fever, breathing trouble, eye/genital involvement, or skin tenderness), I’m most concerned about an acute viral syndrome with mucosal involvement—can you tell me: did you have recent exposure to anyone with a cold/“viral rash” and are you on any immunosuppressants or have any history of herpes/HSV or recurrent mouth ulcers? Doctor: Also, when you say “new cough,” is it dry or productive, and do you have any sore throat, fatigue, or swollen lymph nodes? Doctor: REQUEST TEST: COVID-19/Influenza PCR and a rapid strep test.
RESULTS: COVID-19/Influenza PCR: NORMAL READINGS. Rapid strep test: NORMAL READINGS.

Doctor: Thanks—negative COVID/flu PCR and rapid strep make infection less likely; do you have any recent new meds even short courses (including antibiotics/NSAIDs), or any history of similar rashes, and did the rash start right after you took anything? Also, on exam, do the mouth ulcers look like multiple small shallow ulcers, and do you have any skin pain/“burning” or blisters anywhere on the back?

Patient: I haven’t started any new medications or short courses recently, and I’ve never had a rash like this before. The mouth ulcers are multiple small, shallow, very painful sores, and the back rash doesn’t feel blistering or burn—just red, flat patches.

Doctor: With multiple very painful small mouth ulcers plus a new, non-bistering, non-painful flat red patch rash that began overnight, and with negative COVID/flu PCR and rapid strep, I’m now considering early Stevens–Johnson syndrome / erythema multiforme spectrum versus a severe viral/reactive mucositis—can you tell me if you currently have any eye pain/redness, and whether you have taken any over-the-counter meds in the last 2–6 weeks (including NSAIDs, cold medicines, or supplements)? Doctor: Also, on your back rash: are the patches sharply defined (targets) or just diffuse redness, and do you have any blistering or peeling of skin around any areas? Doctor: If no eye/genital involvement and no blistering/peeling, I’ll treat this as erythema multiforme–type mucositis/viral trigger; if any eye involvement or skin tenderness/skin sloughing appears, we’ll treat as a medical emergency for SJS/TEN—please answer those two points now.

Patient: I don’t have any eye pain or redness, and I haven’t noticed any blistering, skin peeling, or skin tenderness on the rash. The patches are more diffuse red patches rather than sharply defined target lesions. I also haven’t taken any over-the-counter meds or supplements in the last 2–6 weeks.

Doctor: Thank you—no eye symptoms, no blistering/peeling/skin tenderness, and the back lesions are diffuse red patches rather than target-like. Given acute onset (1 day), painful multiple mouth ulcers, negative COVID/flu PCR and rapid strep, and absence of medication exposure or mucocutaneous blistering, my leading diagnosis is erythema multiforme–type mucositis triggered by a viral infection. DIAGNOSIS READY: Erythema multiforme / viral mucositis (minor erythema multiforme spectrum) with acute oral ulceration.
